topic: P&H HC: a wife's domestic violence case under Section 12, DV Act cannot be transferred from the Magistrate to the Family Court just because a maintenance petition (Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS) is pending there - Section 27 makes the Magistrate the competent court; Section 26 only lets DV reliefs be sought in already pending proceedings; convenience or consent cannot create jurisdiction; follows Shaurabh Kumar Tripathi v. Vidhi Rawal (SC), Kerala HC and Delhi HC; Bombay HC (Rohan Shah) took a different view (XXXX v. YYYY, TA No. 24 of 2026, 2026:PHHC:200211, Justice Mandeep Pannu, reported 13-14 Nov 2026)

slides.title: Your **DV case** stays with the Magistrate
slides.subtitle: A pending maintenance case in the Family Court is **not a reason** to move a domestic violence case there, says the Punjab and Haryana High Court.
slides.cite: **XXXX v. YYYY** · 2026:PHHC:200211 · Punjab and Haryana High Court · Justice Mandeep Pannu · reported 13 November 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: Two cases, **two courts**
bullets: A wife filed a domestic violence case under **Section 12 of the DV Act, 2005** before a Judicial Magistrate in Gurugram.
A maintenance case between the same couple (**Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS**) was pending in the Family Court, Gurugram.
The husband asked the High Court to **shift the DV case** to the Family Court, saying the facts and evidence overlap.

slides.label: The law
slides.title: The Act names the **right court**
bullets: **Section 27** of the DV Act makes the Magistrate the competent court for a Section 12 application.
**Section 26** only lets a woman ask for DV reliefs inside a case that is **already pending** in a civil, family or criminal court.
The Court said that limited power does **not** give the Family Court the power to hear a separate DV case.

slides.label: Key point
slides.title: Convenience cannot **create** jurisdiction
bullets: Only the law decides which court can hear a case. **Convenience, cost or even consent** of both sides cannot change that.
Fear of overlapping evidence or conflicting findings cannot override the scheme of the Act.
The Court relied on the **Supreme Court** (Shaurabh Kumar Tripathi) and rulings of the Kerala and Delhi High Courts. The transfer plea was **dismissed**.

slides.label: What it means for you
slides.title: Know **where** your case belongs
bullets: A DV case filed under Section 12 stays before the **Magistrate**, the court the Act names - a pending maintenance case does not change that.
The woman can still ask for DV reliefs in a pending Family Court case under **Section 26**, if she chooses.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.
slides.note: Keep in mind: the Bombay High Court has taken a different view, and this ruling did not decide who is right on the merits of the dispute.

caption:
A maintenance case in the Family Court does not pull your domestic violence case away from the Magistrate 🏛️⚖️

The Punjab and Haryana High Court has refused a husband's request to move his wife's domestic violence case from a Judicial Magistrate in Gurugram to the Family Court, Gurugram. He argued that a maintenance case between the couple was already pending in the Family Court, and that running two cases on overlapping facts would cause confusion and conflicting findings.

The Court explained that under Section 27 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, the Magistrate is the competent court for a Section 12 application. Section 26 only allows a woman to seek DV reliefs inside a case already pending in a civil, family or criminal court. That limited power does not let the Family Court take over a separate DV case. The Court also said that jurisdiction comes only from the law, not from convenience, cost or the consent of the parties.

The Court relied on the Supreme Court's reading of Sections 26 and 27 in Shaurabh Kumar Tripathi v. Vidhi Rawal, and on rulings of the Kerala and Delhi High Courts. It noted that the Bombay High Court had taken a different view. The transfer plea was dismissed, and the parties were told to appear before the Magistrate.

Case: XXXX v. YYYY, TA No. 24 of 2026, 2026:PHHC:200211
Court: Punjab and Haryana High Court, Justice Mandeep Pannu, reported 13 November 2026
